title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
description: The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is
body:
The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is shown electronically on a pump at a QuikTrip station Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Greenwood Village, Colo.
                
                    David Zalubowski/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        David Zalubowski/AP
    

   
   WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.   
   Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.   Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.   
   Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.   Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.   "I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.   
   Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.   Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."   Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal   The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.   
   Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.   A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."   Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."   The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.   Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash   Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.   "It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.   Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."   "This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."   The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.   
   It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.   The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.   Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months   Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.   This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.   The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.   The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.   Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.   
   Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

schema.headline: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms

title: U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
description: A detainee boards a deportation flight o
body:
A detainee boards a deportation flight on GlobalX Air in Minnesota in December 2025.
                
                    Photo by Elizabeth Flores/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Photo by Elizabeth Flores/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images
    

   
   The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation.   A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.   The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.   
   Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.   
   Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House, a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.   Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.   "It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.   The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.   DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.   
   "But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.   
   Facilitating Soliman's return   Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.   " We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."   The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.   Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings.   
   Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.   That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.   The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a  senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.   
   " We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."   The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.   
   Hinderaker's order to return Soliman marks the second time a judge has forced the government to return a third-country migrant from an African nation. A Colorado judge also ordered the return of Brayan Omar Sanchez Servellon, originally from Honduras, who was sent to the Central African Republic earlier this year.

title: Trump's Affordable Suit
description: NPR's Mary Louise Kelly speaks with New York Times fashion reporter Jacob Gallagher about President Trump's apparent choice to wear a suit from
body:
NPR's Mary Louise Kelly speaks with New York Times fashion reporter Jacob Gallagher about President Trump's apparent choice to wear a suit from the budget menswear chain Jos. A. Bank.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  Onstage at a political rally in Nebraska on Monday, President Trump was wearing what he pretty much always wears - dark suit, white shirt, solid tie. But at one point, he stopped, stood still, opened his suit jacket wide and flashed the lining. Cameras clicked, and they captured the tag stitched into that glossy blue lining - Jos. A. Bank. President Trump, a billionaire, wearing an affordable suit - among those intrigued was Jacob Gallagher, fashion reporter at The New York Times. He's on the line from The New York Times newsroom. Hey there, Jacob.JACOB GALLAGHER: Hi.KELLY: Hi. All right, so for people who are not into menswear, not familiar with the brand, describe Jos. A. Bank.GALLAGHER: It's funny that you say not into menswear because Jos. A. Bank is one of those brands that if you're not at all into clothes, you might still know because they are kind of ubiquitous.KELLY: They're at your neighborhood mall often.GALLAGHER: Yeah, exactly. Exactly. They're probably not far from where a lot of your listeners are sitting. There's a Jos. A. Bank chain or location somewhere, and they sell pretty much what you would call an affordable suit, a cheaper suit. They sit on the kind of budget end of the suiting market. That's to say they sell for around $500, I would say, is kind of the median price of a Jos. A. Bank suit. The suit that Trump was wearing appeared to be from its Traveler line, which is right in that kind of 500, $600 price range depending on when you check the Jos. A. Bank store or website because they are the kind of brand that always seems to be running some kind of sale.KELLY: OK. So nothing wrong with a discounted - nothing wrong with...GALLAGHER: No, indeed not.KELLY: ...An affordable suit. But in the past, President Trump has talked about wearing suits from Italian company Brioni. Their suits would cost - what? - something like 10 times that and higher.GALLAGHER: Yeah, just about 10 times that right now. Trump, for years and through his spokespeople, would say that he wore Brioni or sometimes there was a tailor in Brooklyn, Martin Greenfield. He was a custom tailor who dressed a number of presidents. We were always told this kind of, but, you know, obviously, there's not much evidence of him flashing his jacket then to show that they were Brioni.KELLY: You have a great line in your piece. I'm quoting you. If Brioni is a two-Michelin-star meal, Jos. A. Bank is fast food.GALLAGHER: Yeah. And that's really kind of the point here - is it's not like this is - the Jos. A. Bank suit is bad. It's - you know, it'll do the job, so to speak, but it is just quite a different class of suit than what he wore in the past.KELLY: In your story, you raise a question which boils down to, was this political messaging? We're in a hot election season. Elections are upon us, and affordability is very much on voters' minds.GALLAGHER: I think that that could absolutely be a part of this. It's funny because in spite of it being more affordable, I wouldn't say - and this might be splitting hairs - that it's Trump presenting himself in a man-of-the-people kind of way because, obviously, a lot of people in America don't wear suits at all right now.KELLY: Yeah.GALLAGHER: At a Trump rally, there's pretty much always one guy wearing a suit - it's Trump - and that's kind of it. But I also do think that what it does probably boil down to is more so that Jos. A. Bank is a very conservative-looking suit. It's a very traditional cut. It's a larger cut, going back decades. He's really dressed in a very conservative businessman manner from the 1980s.KELLY: No Italian flash here. OK, Jacob, are you ready for the most important question?GALLAGHER: Sure.KELLY: How did the president look? Did he pull off the Jos. A. Bank suit?GALLAGHER: I think Trump at this point - that fit of suit is what clearly he likes. It's obviously not kept up with the times, but I would say, in regards to how Trump looks, he looks standard Trump. And that means it's a bit of a bigger fit, it's a bit boxier, and there's really no shape or cut to it, but it's what you expect him to look like at this point.KELLY: Jacob Gallagher - he covers fashion and style for The New York Times. Thank you.GALLAGHER: Thank you very much.(SOUNDBITE OF MADONNA SONG, "VOGUE")

title: U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court
description: U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court   The U.S. has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, with Secr
body:
U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court   The U.S. has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle the world's only permanent war crimes tribunal.

    
        Politics
    


                  
            October 10, 20267:40 AM ET
         
      

      
      U.S. imposes sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5996606/nx-s1-9959707" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      The U.S. has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle the world's only permanent war crimes tribunal.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  This year's Nobel Peace Prize was meant to bolster international humanitarian law and went to a South African jurist who has worked on the International Criminal Court, among other places. But the Trump administration wants to dismantle that court and accuses it of trying to prosecute Americans. NPR's Michele Kelemen reports on new U.S. sanctions against the world's only standing war crimes tribunal.MICHELE KELEMEN, BYLINE: Secretary of State Marco Rubio calls the ICC a rogue court and says the U.S. is now cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARCO RUBIO: America never joined the court. We don't need that court, and we don't want it.KELEMEN: In a video message, Rubio accused globalist experts - as he called them - of wanting the ICC to go after Americans.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RUBIO: They want the International Criminal Court to do more, including the prosecution of American citizens and service members that are defending their country. They want to prosecute Border Patrol agents that are protecting our nation's borders, and they want to prosecute our elected leaders.KELEMEN: But U.S. personnel are not the subject of any current investigation. The ICC suspended its look into the U.S. role in Afghanistan, even as it continues to prosecute crimes by the Taliban there. The Trump administration has criticized another big case - the arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza. This year's Nobel Peace Prize winner, Navi Pillay, says international law and human rights are under threat. She spoke in Nuremberg, site of the first major international war crimes tribunal against the Nazis.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)NAVI PILLAY: These efforts that we are now seeing, which are attempts to weaken international criminal justice, endanger the progress painstakingly made since Nuremberg.KELEMEN: The president of the International Criminal Court rejected the U.S. sanction, saying the court will not be deterred. The U.S. is giving companies six months to wind down their ties to the court. Indiana University professor David Bosco, who's written a book about the ICC, says this was meant to be a centralized place for war crimes victims to seek justice, instead of having courts for each and every conflict.DAVID BOSCO: That was the - what happened during the 1990s, of course, was they set up, you know, a special court for the Balkans. They set up a special court for Rwanda. And I don't think it makes sense to anybody to do that rather than having a centralized court. The key question is - how broad is the jurisdiction of that court going to be?KELEMEN: The court only has jurisdiction in member states, and that does not include the U.S. Secretary Rubio says he expects U.S. allies who rely on the U.S. military for their defense to, quote, "rein in" the court.Michele Kelemen, NPR News, Washington.

title: Why mailing a ballot close to Election Day may get it rejected for a late postmark
description: A Wake County Board of Elections employe
body:
A Wake County Board of Elections employee prepares a mail-in ballot to be sent out to a voter in September in Raleigh, N.C.
                
                    Matt Ramey/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Matt Ramey/AP
    

   
   Relying on the U.S. Postal Service to return a mail-in ballot close to Election Day now comes with an additional risk for many voters — a late postmark that gets a vote rejected.   The risk stems from mailing system changes that began last year. And those changes have pushed some election officials to encourage voters to consider returning their ballots at their local election office or any available drop boxes instead.   The calls to avoid mailboxes also come as trust in the Postal Service delivering mail ballots on time has fallen, and after President Trump pushed to restrict voting by mail for the midterm elections but was blocked by the Supreme Court.   
   Election officials often use the date of the postmark that USPS stamps on envelopes to determine whether a ballot was sent by Election Day.   About a week before next month's Election Day, USPS says it plans to roll out special postmarking procedures at post offices affected by the changes as part of its "extraordinary measures" policy to boost mail service for federal general elections.   Still, the agency continues to recommend that voters mail back ballots at least a week before their state's deadline. And in states with a grace period for receiving late-arriving mail ballots, USPS recommends stopping by a post office to ask for a manual postmark to make sure a ballot gets postmarked on the same day it's mailed.   How mailing system changes led to the risk of late postmarks   Since April 2025, USPS has been rolling out cuts to daily mail pick-ups and processing changes at certain post offices, especially in rural areas. What USPS calls its "Regional Transportation Optimization" effort is part of a 10-year reorganization plan the agency began in 2021 to try to stabilize its finances.   As a result, USPS may not automatically stamp a date on an envelope the same day it's collected by a letter carrier or dropped off at a post office or a big blue collection box.   
   As part of its "extraordinary measures" for these midterms, USPS has instructed post offices affected by RTO to separate returned ballots from other mail starting Oct. 26 so that managers can manually add postmarks the day the ballots are collected.   
   That procedure was not in place during this year's primary elections, which saw increased ballot rejection rates in multiple states.   Elena Patel, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, says she is encouraged by the steps USPS plans to take in the coming weeks to address concerns about late postmarks.   But the situation is still risky for voters, Patel adds, given that it's not clear how post offices will carry out these directives for the first time, particularly in places where staffing may be stretched.   For the general election, an additional 43,000 to 55,000 ballots around the country could be rejected for arriving late because of the RTO effort, according to a new analysis by Patel, who produced the estimates before USPS announced its final extraordinary measures policy.   "These are some of the realities of running a very large postal network on tight finances," says Patel, who once worked as an economist at the Postal Regulatory Commission.   USPS plans to take other "extraordinary measures" for mail-in ballots   USPS has outlined other extraordinary measures:   Starting Oct. 24, 10 days before Election Day, some post offices may extend their opening and closing times by a half-hour and set up lines or drive-through lanes just for voters who want to get a manual postmark for their mail-in ballot. And starting Oct. 26, USPS says it plans to speed up delivery of ballots.   Asked why it is not starting extraordinary measures 15 days before Election Day, as it did for the 2024 and 2022 elections, USPS said in a statement: "The time period for extraordinary measures is carefully considered in advance of each General Election, and it is based on a number of internal factors. The Postal Service has successfully delivered America's election mail for more than 150 years, and we are confident that we will do so again this year."   
   Still, some eligible voters who rely on voting by mail are between "a rock and a hard place" when trying to navigate the mailing system, says Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, a voter education organization in Alaska.   No post offices in the state are affected by the RTO effort, but Sparck, a member of the Qissunamiut Tribe of Chevak, says she has come across many absentee voters in Alaska Native villages who had their ballots rejected — an outcome that she fears will discourage some from trying to vote again.   "The No. 1 reason for that was postmarking delays. Now, even on a good Alaskan day with no weather challenges, it doesn't mean we're going to have an operational post office on a business day during business hours," Sparck says. "It's always, always easier said than done to kind of go along with the system's rules. But the system doesn't exactly work for us."   For now, Sparck is encouraging eligible voters to make a plan to be an October voter and not wait until November's Election Day if they can.   "If there is an early voting opportunity in a community," Sparck says, "we're asking people to drop their ballots off with those folks so that it becomes part of the chain of custody."   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

title: Republican congressman tries to outrun a potential blue wave in New York toss-up seat
description: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, speaks during a
body:
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, speaks during a press conference in Chappaqua, New York. Lawler is running in a tight race in a toss-up district that could help determine control of Congress.
                
                    Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America
    

   
   ROCKLAND COUNTY, New York – Photos of children and grandchildren line the wall behind the counter at Sparky's Diner, a local joint that sits on the corner of a busy intersection in Garnerville, New York, about an hour outside New York City.   "I've been in this place 50 years, it'll be 51 in February," said Jeannie Nicolakis, the diner's owner. "I started out – I didn't even have my kids at the time – and then I had my kids, and I raised them in here, in a playpen."   But her pride doesn't stop at her family. It extends to her congressman, Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican running for reelection in New York's 17th district. It is one of the closest races in the country in a seat encompassing a string of commuter towns and suburbs around the Hudson River Valley.   
   "He's like my own son. That's how I see him," she said, before adding, "not really my son – because I'm old enough to be his grandmother – but I see him as a grandson that's done so much for this county."   To supporters like Nicolakis, no one can take Lawler's place. But this district is far from a Republican stronghold. It's one of just a handful of places that elected a Republican to the House of Representatives in 2024 and also voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris, a Democrat.   Two years later, Lawler's ability to hold onto the seat could be a deciding factor in determining whether Republicans can keep their narrow majority in the House of Representatives. He faces a competitive challenge from Democrat Cait Conley, a military veteran and former counterterrorism official during the Biden administration who has sought to chip away at the broader coalition that's elected Lawler to congress twice before.   Lawler has tried to position himself as a Republican who is unafraid to cross his own party and highlights examples on the campaign trail, including how he broke with the administration over the decision to end a policy that shielded nearly 350,000 of Haitian migrants from deportation. Lawler says he was able to get the White House to temporarily extend work authorizations for beneficiaries of the program, however that has since expired.   
   He also regularly touts his work to raise the state and local property tax deduction, or SALT cap, a popular issue among his constituents that became a flash point in negotiations over Trump's massive tax and spending bill. Lawler ultimately cast a deciding vote in favor of the legislation, though critics have argued that other key parts of the bill have hurt voters, notably, thesizable cuts to federal healthcare funds.   At the same time, Lawler hasn't shied away from Trump.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, walks on stage on the second day of the Republican National Convention in September.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wong/Getty Images North America
    

   
   "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree, and that's okay. After all, we're both New Yorkers," Lawler said in an address at the Republican National Convention in September. "What I learned about President Trump behind closed doors is that if you're willing to make your case and fight for what you believe in, he's willing to listen."   With less than a month until Election Day, Democrat and Republican-aligned groups have already collectively spent more than $40 million on ad spending in this race.   It comes as national polls show the GOP at a disadvantage, finding that voters are more likely to choose Democrats over Republicans when asked which party's candidate they would back in their district. Plus, President Trump continues to battle historically low approval ratings, with a majority of Americans saying they "strongly disapprove" of his job performance, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll.   Can voters separate Lawler from his party?   Just outside of Sparky's Diner on a recent sunny Saturday afternoon, a lengthy procession of local first-responders and marching bands participate in the annual Rockland County Volunteer Firefighters Association parade. Lawler walks alongside them, frequently stopping to take selfies and shake hands with residents lining nearby sidewalks.   Despite the national stakes of his race, Lawler remains confident in his victory this fall, asserting that his deep understanding of the district makes him the right person to lead it.   
   "Look, all politics is local," he said in an interview as he neared the end of the parade route.   "My constituents know who I am," he said. "The people who are solely voting on the basis of their dislike of Donald Trump, that's their prerogative, that's their right. But the vast majority of my constituents care about the substance of issues and the policy solutions that we can forge. And I'm proud of the record that I've been able to deliver for this district."   But campaigning as an independent voice within Trump's party may be a tough line for the sitting Republican to walk, especially as voters continue to raise alarm bells about the high cost of living.   Across the Hudson River in the town of Armonk, located within the more liberal-leaning Westchester County, Brett Silverstein is one of many parents trying to keep an eye on their kids as they run around the town's fall festival. He cites high energy prices as a top concern.   "You're paying for goods that are inflated because of how much gasoline is and how much diesel is," he said, adding that while he used to vote for Republicans, he doesn't like Trump and in turn remains doubtful of Lawler's message.   "He's supported Trump and kind of the whole 'MAGA train' over the past 2 to 4 years," he said. "So given how he's affiliated with that, I'm just not a big fan of it in general."   It's an association that's pushed away some of the voters that first backed Lawler in 2022, including self-described moderate Mike Monroe, who ended up casting a ballot against the sitting congressman two years later and plans to again this year.   "He's basically the House of Representatives' version of [Maine Republican Sen.] Susan Collins," said Monroe, who lives in the town of Nanuet, part of Rockland County. "[Lawler] stands up to the Trump administration in certain instances, but only when it doesn't matter."   
   Democrats here walk their own political tight rope   Monroe now volunteers for Conley, who's tried to appeal to Democrats as well as disaffected Republicans and Independents on the campaign trail by arguing that Lawler's record in Congress has made New Yorkers worse off.   "Whether it's somebody who's a registered Republican, Independent or Democrat, [it] doesn't matter," Conley said in an interview. "The pain they're feeling is real for all, regardless of political affiliation."   "It's harder to put food on the table, keep a roof over their heads, afford health care, or keep the lights on. And they deserve better. And I will be better," she added.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Cait Conley, the Democrat running against Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, hopes to appeal to Democrats and disaffected Republicans to win in November.
                
                    Spencer Platt/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Spencer Platt/Getty Images North America
    

   
   Conley has also tried to differentiate herself from factions of her party that could turn off swing voters, distancing from high-profile figures on the left like New York City Mayor and democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani. She also hasn't publicly campaigned alongside the state's Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has faced criticism from Lawler and other Republicans in the state particularly over her economic and immigration-related policies.   It's a strategy that could prove helpful for this district where fewer voters are fiercely partisan.   "A lot of swing districts are just swing districts because they're equal number of Democrats and Republicans. That's not really what's going on in NY-17," said Evan Roth Smith, a democratic pollster who runs the firm Slingshot Strategies.   Polling conducted by Slingshot shows that between 30 and 40 percent of voters in the district are either ticket splitters or are only loosely partisan in their personal identification with the parties.   "One cycle they might vote for a Republican, the next cycle they might vote for a Democrat," Roth Smith said. "So it's a swing district because there are a lot of swing voters."   That's the case for retired builder Michael Alvarado, who lives in Stony Point, a town farther north within Rockland.   
   "I vote for whoever thinks my way," he said. "I don't really have a party. I'm not a Republican or a Democrat. Actually I would say I'm more of a Democrat than a Republican."   Though he says he supported Lawler last time, he's still deciding this year, and cares most about backing a candidate who is pro union and will cut school and property taxes.   When asked if anyone is currently speaking to those concerns, Alvarado replies, "not really," but added, he always votes.   "I'm just looking. See what happens come November. We'll hear all the promises."

title: Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
description: Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
body:
Week in Politics: Hegseth's livestream backlash; Greece ambassador Guilfoyle scandal
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5995114/nx-s1-9959897" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Bipartisan blowback on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plans to livestream a military execution, plus a scandal involving Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US Ambassador to Greece.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  There has been pointed and bipartisan objection to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan to livestream a military execution. The Pentagon announced this week that Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad in December. He is the former Fort Hood Army psychiatrist who fatally shot 13 people and wounded nearly three dozen others in 2009. NPR senior contributor Ron Elving joins us. Ron, thanks so much for being with us.RON ELVING, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.SIMON: Secretary Hegseth told Real America's Voice that, quote, "it's public because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things." But many in his own Republican Party disagree, aren't they?ELVING: They say it's a bad idea - beyond disgusting, in the words of Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican senator, whose vote enabled Hegseth's confirmation last year. They're saying it's medieval, even barbaric, comparing it to public executions by ISIS and other terrorists or radical regimes such as the Taliban and Afghanistan.But let's be clear - the issue now after all these years is not crime and punishment. The 2009 crime is beyond dispute, and even those with the deepest doubts about the death penalty itself see its rationale and its application in this case. The dispute now is over making a spectacle of it. No U.S. serviceman has been put to death since 1961, back before the Vietnam escalation. And no American has been executed publicly since 1936 - nine decades ago.Hegseth says the livestream will send a signal that there are consequences, but does anyone think someone who did what Nidal Hasan did thought his actions wouldn't have consequences? This is tantamount to saying global terrorists need to be reminded that suicide bombing has downside risks. Trump was asked about this spectacle, said he gave it the green light, absolutely. But Vice President JD Vance said yesterday there were weeks ago before the December 3 date, and things could change.SIMON: Also this week, The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, asked a Trump donor to send her $100,000 to cover credit card debt just before her confirmation hearings last year, and to do it secretly. Is the ambassador's goose cooked?ELVING: Well, the water's certainly hot enough. It depends on the call of the chef as to whether it's become too hot. The president said it was too bad but said little else. And the unseemly request for 100,000 and the access to the Trumps that was at issue will add further to the narrative of corruption surrounding the Oval Office and the first family in general in this second term.Guilfoyle first came in contact with the Trump operation as a news personality on television. She was considered a catch because 20 years ago, she had been married to California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, a Democrat. And she later became engaged to Donald Trump Jr. during his father's first term and was seen with him at the party's 2024 convention, but that relationship ended later that year. Trump Jr. has subsequently married someone else.The main issue of this midterm election, Scott, as we know, is affordability. The issue of government corruption and abuse of public trust, though, is rising fast. And if voters come to link what they don't like in the economy with what they don't like to hear about administration figures selling access, that would add more jet fuel to the anti-incumbent flames.SIMON: Some serious debates this week in battleground states for the midterms - Maine, Michigan, Georgia and Iowa. What stood out to you?ELVING: The common theme was the struggle Republican nominees were in with Trump's tariffs and Trump's war with Iran. They were hamstrung by their need to show independence from those policies, even as they maintained support for the president and the party. At this point, it's clear that Republicans are hoping the Democrats have peaked and the numbers will balance out again. But Republicans are also fearful that the Democrats have not yet peaked and the next round of polls will find them pulling away toward big gains in the House and perhaps a new majority in the Senate.SIMON: NPR's Ron Elving. Thanks so much.ELVING: Thank you, Scott.

title: On the ground in Ohio's 9th District: The battleground shaping next month's midterms
description:
Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Did you vote two years ago, may we ask?WILLIAM WATKINS: Did I vote two years ago?
body:
Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Did you vote two years ago, may we ask?WILLIAM WATKINS: Did I vote two years ago? I actually don't remember. Wow. Oh, yeah. I did. I voted. And I'm regretting my vote right now. I voted for Trump.SIMON: We begin this hour in Ohio, a critical battleground in next month's midterm elections. We visited the state's 9th Congressional District, including city of Toledo. And when we asked people in diners, machine shops, and on streets what they were most concerned about, one worry kept coming up.WATKINS: Oh, the cost of gas is outrageous.THOMAS HAMILTON: And it was over $4 a gallon there for a while, so my car's broke down. I've been riding the bus.TAMYRA FRAZIER: Gas, for sure.SIMON: William Watkins has been working in factories and making deliveries and recently enrolled in a machining class at Toledo's Cherry Street Mission, a nonprofit support group.(SOUNDBITE OF METAL SQUEAKING)SIMON: He hopes to land a better-paying job with steady benefits and is raising a young daughter.WATKINS: Oof. Jesus. This economy has been rough. Like, it's bad. I had a truck. Like, I'd rather walk sometimes than take that truck where I'm going. I remember when I first learned how to drive. Gas was $2. I'm like, I'm not buying no $2 gas. I would darn near cross five highways to get $2 gas right now.SIMON: We asked why he voted for Donald Trump in 2024.WATKINS: I just felt like, with him being the businessman that he was, that he would be able to help the country out a little better. I don't want to say I was wrong. But us common folk that go to work every day and work hard for our money on a normal job - it's really hurting our pockets.HAMILTON: This one right here is going to be for our cup holders or our coasters. Excuse me.SIMON: Thomas Hamilton is in the same machining class. He's separated from his partner and trying to support five boys.HAMILTON: If I got to work two and three jobs, plus come here, I don't get to see my kids. You know, that's not a benefit for them. That's hurting them 'cause now they got to grow up without a father around. Trump seems to me like - a lot of the principles and stuff that I seen when he first took office, and everything sounded good - everything sounded great - you know, it's just kind of fizzled out. I don't think he really has kept his word.(SOUNDBITE OF CASH REGISTER RINGING)UNIDENTIFIED CASHIER: Twelve,13, 14, 15, 20.UNIDENTIFIED CUSTOMER: All right. Thanks a lot.UNIDENTIFIED CASHIER: Thank you.UNIDENTIFIED CUSTOMER: Thank you, everyone.UNIDENTIFIED CASHIER: See you later.SIMON: There are 19 pies on the menu at Schmucker's diner in Toledo, from apple pie to strawberry rhubarb. Michael Crockett is a retired factory worker and is having breakfast with his grown daughter, Zhane. She says she often has to figure out what to do without.ZHANE CROCKETT: I would say, like, a year ago, it was $35 for a full tank? Now I'm paying about $55, $60 to fill up. So that's eating away.MICHAEL CROCKETT: I've controlled my lifestyle. I think I got it down to a science. I eat one time a day. But that came with getting older, and I found out that eating isn't necessarily my best friend because I overeat. So that's how I cut down on my budget (laughter).SIMON: President Trump won many traditionally Democratic working-class votes from Ohioans over three elections. But Tamyra Frazier of Toledo, who works two jobs in home and healthcare to support her daughter and voted for President Trump in 2024, now says...FRAZIER: He started wars - wars that did not need to be started. I feel like Trump should just - don't stick his nose in other people's business. He should just stay and worry. We got so much work to do with our own people.SIMON: Early voting opened this week. Outside of a polling station in Defiance, Ohio, about an hour from Toledo, we met Jerry Brittsan, who had just cast his vote. He wore a hat in the autumn sun that said, veteran.JERRY BRITTSAN: I support the president. And I think that when you look at the stock market and all these other type things, I think the country is on a rebound.SIMON: What would you say to people who say, look, you know, the price of gas. I'm working two and three jobs. It's hard to commute between jobs. I have to spend much more money than I did before on food. This is making uncomfortable choices for me and my family.BRITTSAN: I think it's going to be temporary, although, from the oil-and-gas-type thing, I think that's going to change.SIMON: Another early voter, Angela Hearne, told us that taxes were the most important issue to her. But also...ANGELA HEARNE: People's lifestyle? I don't care. But don't impress it on me - that kind of stuff. I can live here fine and happy. But I don't need to know your religion or your sexual whatever. I don't care. I don't care who you pray to. I don't. But don't have to express it on to me.SIMON: And that helped you...HEARNE: Yes.SIMON: ...Make your decision to vote...HEARNE: Oh, yes.SIMON: ...One way or another. Yeah.HEARNE: Yes.SIMON: What about an issue like inflation, the cost of living?HEARNE: That also. We always lived within our means 'cause that's the way we was brought up. So we always kind of watched our Ps and Qs. If we couldn't afford it, we didn't buy it.SIMON: Do you think the war in Iran is helping your family or America?HEARNE: Personally, right now, this - no. It isn't. But maybe later on, it will be.SIMON: There are statewide races for Ohio's governorship and a Senate seat, which current polls show to be close. Marcy Kaptur has represented the 9th Congressional District since 1983. She still lives in her childhood home in Toledo and is the longest-serving woman in the history of the U.S. Congress. But a Republican-controlled state legislature redrew her district lines. President Trump won it by seven points in 2024, though Representative Kaptur was reelected.The district has been redrawn again by the legislature. And Cook Political Report rates this year's congressional race between Kaptur and former Republican Ohio State Representative Derek Merrin a toss-up. The Merrin campaign didn't return our request for an interview. But at Bud's diner on 2nd Street, we ran into...MIKE MCCANN: Mike McCann. I'm the mayor of the city of Defiance, Ohio.SIMON: Bud's is part of the mayor's daily rounds, where pumpkin and Ohio apple pies have just been put on the menu. The mayor's a Republican and hands out a business card that has three direct phone numbers.MCCANN: You know, since I've been mayor, we went from about 16,700 folks to probably around 17,100 right now.SIMON: What are the big issues here at the moment? What has people talking, and what are they worried about?MCCANN: I think the same thing that everybody's talking about. Fuel prices are still high. Now, the state of Ohio just put a 90-day rollback on all their gas taxes, which reduced the price of gas by about $0.40 a gallon. That helps. Certainly, that helps. But it's a 90-day rollback, and we aren't collecting gas tax right now. So what are we going to do when it comes time to...SIMON: Yeah.MCCANN: ...Pave our roads and build our bridges and all those things?SIMON: Are you in accord with the Republican Party nationally? I mean, I don't - I...MCCANN: I can...SIMON: I'm speaking...MCCANN: Yeah.SIMON: Yeah. I mean, I'm covering it. How...MCCANN: Yeah.SIMON: What do you think of President...MCCANN: I...SIMON: ...Trump as running things (ph)?MCCANN: I never agree with everybody on everything.SIMON: Yeah.MCCANN: Locally, people don't agree with everything that we're doing here.SIMON: Coming up to these midterms, President Trump says, I want people to think that my name is on the ballot.MCCANN: I heard that over the weekend.SIMON: Good idea, from your point of view?MCCANN: I - you know, I am not a political strategist. I'll be honest with you. I...SIMON: You've been elected mayor three times. You're doing pretty well.MCCANN: Well, I guess nobody else wants the job (laughter). I will say...SIMON: Yeah.MCCANN: A couple of years ago, when Trump was on the ballot, that's the most activity that I've seen at my polling location where I work, ever. And people were coming in the door, saying, hey. I'm just here to vote for Trump, and then I'll get out of here.SIMON: And as we spoke...MCCANN: Marcy Kaptur just walked in.SIMON: Two longtime Ohio pawls (ph) of different parties shook hands.MARCY KAPTUR: Hi. Hello.MCCANN: Good morning.KAPTUR: Good morning.MCCANN: It was nice to see you.KAPTUR: Good to see you.MCCANN: Everything OK?KAPTUR: Everything's good.MCCANN: You're doing OK?KAPTUR: Yes. I'm doing all right.MCCANN: All right.KAPTUR: Yeah.MCCANN: We've been worried...KAPTUR: I'm healing.MCCANN: ...About you. Yeah.KAPTUR: Thank you. Thank you...MCCANN: I saw...KAPTUR: ...For the primrose (ph).MCCANN: ...The car. I don't know how you survived.KAPTUR: They - it was a miracle.MCCANN: Yeah.KAPTUR: It really was.MCCANN: You definitely had a guy...KAPTUR: I said...MCCANN: ...On your side.KAPTUR: ...I better do my job.(LAUGHTER)SIMON: Marcy Kaptur survived a car accident in August and is now back on the campaign trail.KAPTUR: We live in kind of a crooked state, but that isn't the case here. So I'm just very proud of what I've learned here. The mayor's helped teach me - hardworking people.SIMON: I mean, there's something I've got to say. We have a Democrat and a Republican standing here, getting along, complimenting each other. And the smell of pumpkin pie...KAPTUR: (Laughter).SIMON: ...In this diner is overwhelming. I think a lot of people are going to be saying, this is what America...MCCANN: Yeah.SIMON: ...Should be.MCCANN: This is what I was talking to you about earlier. We all need to put the politics aside and do what's best for our city, do what's best for our county, do what's best for our state and do what's best for our country.KAPTUR: We're rebuilding the steel industry. We're rebuilding the automotive industry. We're bringing in new industry, and we've got a long way to go. And we hope Washington and the financial centers start to see the Great Lakes cities again. They ignored them for a very long time.(SOUNDBITE OF METAL SQUEAKING)SIMON: And back at the machinist workshop, William Watkins is still thinking over who we'll vote for.WATKINS: This country has become more costly with the inflation and tariffs and all that. I mean, hopefully it fits us better in the end. But as of right now, it's rough.SIMON: Yeah.WATKINS: Whatever candidate they do pick, I hope they just have the people in mind because at the end of the day, the people make our nation.SIMON: William Watkins of Toledo, Ohio - one of the voters who will decide the direction of the next U.S. Congress. Our story was produced by Danny Hensel and edited by Martin Patience. And Bud's Ohio apple pie was just terrific.(SOUNDBITE OF WILCO SONG, "MANY WORLDS")

title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
description: Democrats are trying to rebuild trust am
body:
Democrats are trying to rebuild trust among Latino voters, and turning to content creators for help. Above, Spanish language voting stickers which read "He Votado Hoy" ("I Voted Today") at a Philadelphia polling place in 2019.
                
                    Matt Rourke/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Matt Rourke/AP
    

   
   Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.   That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.   This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.   One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.   
   "We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.   That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.   She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.   "My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.   
   Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.   BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.    
   Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.   "So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., chairs BOLD PAC. She says content creators can help bridge a gap for her party. Above, Sanchez speaks on immigration at the U.S. Capitol on May 10, 2023.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.   Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.    "One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.   In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.   It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.   
   This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.   Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.   "Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.   Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.   
   So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.   
   "Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.   So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.   "My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.   Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.   "The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.
